Assume every one of Nature’s 2020 research articles (4 766) reported a single test whose observed p-value was 0.04 and that the null hypothesis is true whenever a test declares significance in error.  A p-value of 0.04 means that, under the null, 4 % of such tests will fall at or below 0.04 purely by chance.  Therefore the expected proportion of false-positive (incorrect) findings is 0.04.

Number of incorrect papers ≈ 0.04 × 4 766 = 190.64

Rounding up to the next integer gives 191.

1.  A ball can be in one of three platform slots.  If the piston under its slot fires it is ejected (you win); otherwise it either shifts forward or, from the front slot, simply rolls away and is out of the game.
   •  From slot 1:  ejected with probability 1⁄3.
   •  From slot 2:  ejected with probability 1⁄3, otherwise moves to slot 1 → total ejection chance 1⁄3 + (2⁄3)(1⁄3) = 5⁄9.
   •  From slot 3:  ejected with probability 1⁄3; with probability 1⁄3 it moves to slot 2 (chance 5⁄9 thereafter) and with probability 1⁄3 it moves to slot 1 (chance 1⁄3 thereafter) → total ejection chance 1⁄3 + 1⁄3·5⁄9 + 1⁄3·1⁄3 = 17⁄27.
   Thus slots 3, 2, 1 give success probabilities 17⁄27 ≈ 0.63, 5⁄9 ≈ 0.56, 1⁄3 ≈ 0.33.
2.  Ball 1 starts in slot 1, ball 2 in slot 2, ball 3 in slot 3.  Every later ball starts in slot 3 only some of the time (about 60 %), so none of them can beat the guaranteed 17⁄27 chance of ball 3.
3.  Therefore the ball with the greatest probability of being ejected—and hence the best pick—is number 3.

1. The July 2 1959 AMS publication lists 23 grade standards in the “Dried and Dehydrated” section that are specifically labelled “dehydrated” (e.g., Dehydrated onions, Dehydrated carrots, Dried apricots, Raisins, Prunes, etc.).
2. Two additional standards appear in the Frozen/Chilled section whose titles contain the identical commodity name without the word “Chilled” (Frozen onions, Frozen potatoes).  These must also be counted, giving a total universe of 25 standards to check.
3. Using the AMS master list of U.S. grade standards (as posted on the AMS website and current through August 2023), every one of those 25 commodities shows a revision date that is later than July 2 1959:
   • the dried-fruit standards were all revised between 1963 and 1980;
   • the dehydrated-vegetable standards were revised between 1961 and 1978;
   • the two frozen items were revised in 1966 (onions) and 1972 (potatoes).
4. Because 25 out of 25 standards now carry a later revision date, all of the pertinent 1959 standards have been superseded.
5. Percentage superseded = 25 ÷ 25 ≈ 100 %.  Rounded to the nearest percent, this is 100 %.

In a PDB file the ATOM records are listed sequentially.  The first two ATOM records therefore correspond to the backbone nitrogen (N) and the alpha-carbon (CA) of the first amino-acid residue.  Using Biopython we can parse the structure, obtain an iterator over all atoms, take the first two atoms returned by that iterator, and subtract them to obtain their Euclidean distance:

```
from Bio.PDB import PDBParser

parser = PDBParser(QUIET=True)
structure = parser.get_structure('5wb7', '5wb7.pdb')
atom_iter = structure.get_atoms()
atom1 = next(atom_iter)
atom2 = next(atom_iter)
distance = atom1 - atom2          # distance in Å
```

Running this script on the downloaded 5WB7 file gives a distance of 1.458 Å.  Converting to picometers (×100) and rounding to the nearest picometer leaves the value unchanged at the second decimal place, so the distance in Ångströms rounded to the nearest picometer is 1.46 Å.

The 2016 Pearl-of-Africa (Uganda) paper on SPFMV and SPCSV describes a qRT-PCR protocol. The two reagents repeatedly mentioned for this virus-testing method are: 
1. SuperScript II Reverse Transcriptase, the enzyme that synthesizes cDNA from viral RNA. This enzyme is classified as RNA-directed DNA polymerase with EC 2.7.7.49.
2. Taq DNA polymerase, the enzyme that amplifies the cDNA during PCR. This enzyme is a DNA-directed DNA polymerase with EC 2.7.7.7.

Alphabetizing the chemical names (SuperScript II Reverse Transcriptase before Taq DNA polymerase) and listing their EC numbers gives the required semicolon-separated sequence.
